title: The pseudo-inverse from the SVD
summary: Build A⁺ from the SVD and see that A⁺b is the smallest best fit.

blocks.title: The singular values

define.meaning: $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$, where the $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $A^\mathsf{T}A$. Its unit eigenvectors are the right singular vectors $v_i$.

blocks.why: The SVD is the rotate, stretch, rotate you already know. For this $A$ it shows exactly which direction $A$ can't see.
blocks.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\1&2\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $A^\mathsf{T}A = \begin{bmatrix}3&6\\6&12\end{bmatrix}$. Find its eigenvalues, largest first.
hints: The eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
The determinant is 0, so one eigenvalue is 0.

blocks.title: v₁
blocks.why: $v_1$ is the input direction $A$ stretches most; here it is the only one $A$ sees at all.
blocks.prompt: Find $v_1$, the unit eigenvector of $A^\mathsf{T}A$ for $\lambda = 15$.

answer.acceptNote: Either sign is right: singular vectors are only fixed up to sign.

slips.say: The right direction. Now make it a unit vector: divide by its length.

hints: Write $v = (x, y)$. The first row gives $-12x + 6y = 0$, so $y = 2x$.
The direction is $(1, 2)$, and its length is $\sqrt5$.

check.say: A unit vector has $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. And the first row of $A^\mathsf{T}A\,v_1$ should be 15 times $x$.

blocks.title: u₁
blocks.why: $u_1$ is where $A$ sends $v_1$, scaled to unit length: $A v_1 = \sigma_1 u_1$.

answer.acceptNote: The sign goes with $v_1$'s: if you flipped $v_1$, $u_1$ flips too.

hints: Each row of $A$ is $(1, 2)$, so each entry of $A v_1$ is $(1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2)/\sqrt5$.

blocks.title: A⁺

define.meaning: $A^+ = V\,\Sigma^+\,U^\mathsf{T}$. $\Sigma^+$ turns each non-zero $\sigma$ into $1/\sigma$ and leaves each zero as zero.

blocks.why: Undo the stretch where $A$ stretches, and send the invisible direction to zero rather than infinity. That rule is what makes $A^+b$ the smallest best fit.
blocks.prompt: $A$ has rank 1, so $A^+ = \frac{1}{\sigma_1}\,v_1 u_1^\mathsf{T}$. Write it as a $2 \times 3$ matrix.

widget.name: svd-geometry
widget.caption: A $2 \times 2$ example. Drag $\sigma_2$ down to 0: the ellipse flattens, and $A^+$ uses $1/\sigma$ where it can and 0 where $\sigma = 0$.

hints: $v_1 u_1^\mathsf{T}$ is a column times a row: a $2 \times 3$ matrix.

check.say: Row 2 should be twice row 1. And $A A^+ A$ gives back $A$: try its top-left entry.

blocks.title: A⁺b
blocks.why: This is the pseudo-inverse's answer to the least-squares problem.
hints: Row 1 of $A^+$ dotted with $b$, then row 2.
Row 2 of $A^+$ is twice row 1, so its answer is twice as big.
blocks.solution: Your answer from the last lesson. The pseudo-inverse returns the smallest best fit.

blocks.title: v₂
blocks.why: $v_2$ is the direction with $\sigma_2 = 0$. What $A^+$ does to it explains the whole lesson.
blocks.prompt: Find $v_2$, the unit eigenvector of $A^\mathsf{T}A$ for $\lambda = 0$.

slips.say: The right direction. Now make it a unit vector.

blocks.solution: $v_2$ is your null direction $d$, made unit length. $A^+b = \frac{1}{\sigma_1}(u_1 \cdot b)\,v_1$ has no $v_2$ part at all, because $\Sigma^+$ puts a 0 there. No null-space part is exactly what made $p$ the smallest best fit.

sideQuest.title: Check it in numpy
sideQuest.body:
Only if you want to.

```
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 2], [1, 2]])
b = np.array([1, 2, 6])
print(np.linalg.pinv(A))      # rows 1/15 and 2/15
print(np.linalg.pinv(A) @ b)  # [0.6 1.2]
```
